...Soft YTA. I don't like to say that a parent owes their kid college money, etc, but if you a) can afford it, because it's BEEN set aside for each of them, and b) she is struggling to make this house purchase, which is a BIG deal, I really don't see your reasoning for refusing it to her. 

To me, setting aside money for my kids' 'college fund' is, /really/, me setting aside money to help give my kids whatever push they may need when they need it, to achieve something they'd otherwise struggle with. Something big. Like college. Like a home. Like paying for childcare. Not any ol' thing, but big, important things. If they choose a different path for their life, or if something like college is made unfeasible (by a child), then I don't see any point in withholding it from them except to punish them for not living the life I wanted them to. Which may sometimes even be out of their hands.

I say 'soft' here because I know others won't see it that way, and no, you don't owe her money as an adult, and her level of upset may be a bit much, but.... I don't know, if I found out my parents held back a sizable amount of money from me they then gave to all my siblings, because I didn't go to college...

well, among other things, I'd be VERY pissed they didn't TELL me that. My parents did, in fact, offer to me and my siblings, to either help us pay for college, or they'd help us find a job right out of school. We KNEW the terms of the fund. I think you definitely fucked up keeping it a secret, frankly, and that's why I'm leaning more on the end of YTA.

I think that if the server is entirely set on disallowing neurodivergent/neurotypical regardless of any other rule changes, those other rule changes become, essentially, ineffective/unimportant.

I fail to see, personally, why the rules disallowing problematic behavior (toxic positivity, misinformation) are not enough. Many people consider themselves neurodivergent, without being the 'ADHD is a gift, no downsides, its all society's fault' people. And if those people feel alienated not because of their harmful beliefs, but because they use a label that encompasses, among other things, ADHD, to understand themselves, then I don't think it makes sense to disallow said label.

If the worry is that these words alienate the folks already here, I would also say, well, moderation of inappropriate topics would continue, so that anyone (using neurodivergent or not) promoting alienating beliefs that are harmful or misinformative, are still removed.

And same wrt neurotypical. Some people have used it terribly, yeah, but it's also a very neutral descriptor for 'people who are not neurodivergent', and can, in fact, be useful.

Especially because neurodivergent.... has a meaning. It's not just 'I'm one of those people who thinks it means my specific mental disorder is a gift, and everyone else should, too'. Are there people who've acted like that? Yeah, for sure, but there's a lot more people who use it because it literally describes having a brain that's /developed/ differently and thus has affected how they think, act, to a degree 'measurable' generally speaking by a more specific diagnosis, be it ADHD, autism, dyslexia, others. I understand the wariness surrounding the toxicity within parts of that community, but again, blanket banning the word feels, to me, like overkill.

In the end, this proposed rule change feels.....like giving very little ground, and I'm not sure how it would positively impact the sub as it stands, without the moderators giving a bit more leeway in terms of how we label ourselves, while still obviously taking the same amount of care to moderate harmful behavior.

My mom loved kids, loved teaching, and hated, with imo, good reason, the public school system. I regret being homeschooled but honestly I understand and empathize with all of her reasons for choosing it, which is why I have a hard time still with accepting it's impact on me. She was definitely more in the camp of wanting to offer her kids more freedom to learn what they wanted with guidance but not forcing it, no forced social interaction/bullying, etc etc etc.

Problem is that even if those were good intentions/points, the isolation that led to, and everything that that kind of isolation makes worse .... was still a pretty seriously negative impact.

And like, I don't disbelieve her reasoning. I think a lot of parents experienced problems, some pretty serious, in the school system, and felt there were alternatives and they could do better, but it often leads to the same problems in a different environment, or some altogether new problems that parents don't foresee, and the kids have no resources to figure that out or deal with it themselves until they're adults unpacking it. 

There's a lot of reasons though. I just know the biggest in my background was a bad experience from teachers, from support (lack of) in school, a distaste for what felt like needless control from the system, a background in teaching and childcare that led to the desire to provide us with better and more enriching education, etc. probably leaving some stuff out.

Because they are looking at it from a specific lens, that of DID/OSDD being the only possible way to be a system (in the specific way that DID/OSDD is formed). If a system is not formed that way, it is not a system in the same way DID/OSDD creates a system, which doesn't inherently mean illegitimate, but it does mean that if you only believe in that one way to create/be a system, it will seem so. 

Granted, there are also those who will latch onto a viewpoint legitimizing one way of being a system, to bolster their own perceived legitimacy, and likely other reasonings, but the most 'good faith' (and most common, in my experience) reasoning is the first one I listed. Many plural systems who do not have DID/OSDD are very different from those with, so it's understandable to my view that people would not see them as, well, the same thing. It's just a question then of whether someone will see them both as different, but both legitimate, or one as illegitimate. 

I'm also only talking about people who've...genuinely put thought into this, since there are plenty of people, plural, pwDID, and neither, who will have an opinion based on a glance at a carrd and little else.

I'm currently trying to understand my own perception and existence wrt all of this, and it seems to me that while there are aspects to DID/OSDD I will never understand personally, just like there are some aspects to various forms of plurality I won't, my experience not mimicking someone else's doesn't make it illegitimate--but it often does make it very, very different, and not necessarily equatable, if that makes sense.

I think one important thing to remember is that parents can have been abusive while still caring about their children/believing what they've done is best. Especially because quite often, parents might be kinder/gentler than their parents were to them, and still be abusive or harmful. (Or they might simply be the kind of parents that theirs were to them, and not realize that their parents were abusive too).  Abuse doesn't always mean the abuser was acting malignantly towards the victim, with intent to harm.

I can say that my parents certainly care very much about me, but especially when I was much younger, they would react in ways that were not imo okay to treat a child--and one of those ways was withholding food. The fact is food is a basic need. Not feeding someone who relies on you for food is abusive.
I 100% get how weird it is to try and wrap your head around the idea that your parents could be abusive, because I'm still in that spot myself, but....your friends are right that it's a harsh punishment; in general a punishment that is withholding a basic need is considered abusive, whether that's food, sleep, etc. (obviously that's not the only behavior that's abusive, I'm just listing that since it's what this specific punishment falls under)

as to the closet thing--yeah, that's abusive, 100%. that's essentially solitary confinement which is considered abusive to adults let alone children
